4853-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Sluys and its mixed Dutch and English garrison open this 1587 volume, and John Lothrop Motley shows a town lost for want of relief. Williams writes to the queen from the besieged port, schemes to relieve it fail, and Parma enters after the capitulation, enraging Leicester and angering Elizabeth against his critics.

Norris, Wilkes, and Buckhurst pay for the failure, while Drake sails for Spain and strikes at Cadiz and Lisbon, only to be rebuked by Elizabeth. Motley moves between a small port's fate and a famous sea raid, linking them through the queen's temper and the alliance's strains. The volume shows how one surrender echoed through two courts.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1587c:
Chapter sixteen of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands describes the siege of Sluys. Sluys stands on a mere riband of dry land, a strong rampart with many towers. Its detached citadel looks toward the sea; the ravelin of St. Anne looks toward Bruges. Below the streets, vast cellars stored the foreign wines of its trading days.

A Dutch and English garrison holds the town while Leicester and the States dispute eternally. Williams, the Welsh commander, writes for help that faction delays. Parma closes in with his usual method. Motley makes the reader feel the geography: water, mud, and one dry path for relief. The fall of such places decided the war's map. This chapter is siege writing at its most patient, where a town's wine cellars and sea walls matter more than speeches.
podcast-joerogan-ViWvAnvT17c:
Dr. Cornel West joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1325. West is a philosopher and public voice known for fiery talks on justice, race, and faith, delivered in a preacher's rhythm. His visit brings a prophetic style unlike any other guest in the show's run.

West ranges over American life, from the legacy of slavery to the failures of both parties, always returning to love and truth as duties. Rogan mostly listens, asking him to go deeper where the fire rises. The episode is a sermon and a seminar at once, and it shows the studio at its most serious.
podcast-joerogan-dre-5Zy4f7c:
Jeremy Corbell and George Knapp bring the UFO beat to episode 2028 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Corbell makes films from leaked military footage. Knapp, the Las Vegas reporter, has covered Area 51 since he first aired Bob Lazar in 1989. Their joint visits are status reports on disclosure.

They update Rogan on the newest footage and testimony they trust, and on the mood in Washington. Rogan asks what the endgame of the slow leak might be. The episode is a field briefing from the two men who have done the most to keep the subject in the news, full of names, dates, and graded claims.
podcast-tuckercarlson-nxxg3HSlH7c:
Tucker Carlson opens his show by naming the right's daily fight over who gets a platform. Each morning, he says, the feud over labels and bans resumes. He insists the fight did not start with one podcast guest.

Carlson traces the split to closed-door clashes since January. The title calls it an Israel-first meltdown. He asks what future the America First movement has. The episode is part history and part warning. It speaks to viewers caught between two camps and unsure which side still speaks for them. He names names and dates as he goes.
uslaw-usc-t2-s137c:
Section 137c of Title 2 of the United States Code extends a library privilege to two federal courts in Washington. The Library of Congress lends books under set regulations to certain high officials.

This section names the judges of the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. It also names the judges of the District Court for the District of Columbia. Chief judges and associate judges alike are covered. They are authorized to use and take books from the Library of Congress. They do so in the same manner, and under the same regulations, as justices of the Supreme Court.
uslaw-usc-t2-s287c:
Section 287c of Title 2 of the United States Code covers pay for the Office of the Parliamentarian of the House. It sits in Chapter 9C of that title, on that office. Part (a) fixes the pay of the Parliamentarian. He is to be paid at a yearly gross rate set by the Speaker. That rate may not pass the greater of two sums named in the text.

The first sum named is 173,900 dollars. The second is the rate of pay in force for the post under an order of the Speaker made under section 4532 of the title. Part (b) deals with the staff of the office other than the Parliamentarian. Their yearly gross rates are fixed by the Parliamentarian. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s907c:
Section 907c of Title 2 allows flexibility inside defense accounts when deficit cuts are ordered. The setting is the chapter on emergency powers to eliminate budget deficits. Under the conditions the section sets, budget authority for defense programs may be cut deeper than the amount a presidential order specifies.

The deeper cuts may fall on programs, projects, or activities in the defense function. Military personnel accounts are excepted from this treatment. Where extra cuts yield extra savings in outlays, the President may soften cuts elsewhere in the same function. The softening is capped so that added spending does not exceed the added savings. No single program may be raised above its ordered level by this route. The section sits in Chapter 20 of Title 2. The hosted Code text is current through Public Law 119-134. It is a pressure valve inside a rigid cut regime.
